title: Bhujyu asks where the Parikshitas went (3.3)
hook: the third challenger brings a question he got from a spirit, and already knows the answer
tomorrow: Ushasta: "the self within all — show me"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Artabhaga asked what doesn't leave a person at death: the name. And then, in private, karma. Your line was the name.

The third challenger opens with a ghost story. When I was a student, says Bhujyu, we wandered to a house in the land of the Madras. The householder's daughter was possessed by a spirit, a gandharva. We asked it who it was, and it told us its name. Then we asked it about the ends of the world, and where the Parikshitas went. So, Yajnavalkya, I'm asking you: where did the Parikshitas go? It's a trap with the answer already in his pocket. He heard it from a spirit. Let's see if this man knows it too.
screen: `A SPIRIT IN A STUDENT'S STORY.` → `IT KNEW THE ENDS OF THE WORLD.` → `WHERE DID THE PARIKSHITAS GO?`

segments.voice: Who were the Parikshitas? The family of King Parikshit, remembered as great performers of the horse sacrifice, the one that opened this Upanishad two weeks ago. The Mahabharata tells of a Parikshit too: Arjuna's grandson, born after the war. The Upanishad doesn't explain any of that; it assumes its listeners know. Yajnavalkya answers without a pause. The spirit told you, surely, they went where those who perform the horse sacrifice go. And where is that? Then he gives a map. This world is as wide as thirty-two days of the sun's chariot. The earth surrounds it, twice as wide. The ocean surrounds the earth, twice as wide again. And between them is a gap as thin as the edge of a razor, or the wing of a fly. Through that gap, Indra, taking the form of a bird, handed the Parikshitas to the wind, and the wind carried them to where the horse-sacrificers are. Then the key line: so wind is each single thing, and wind is everything together. Whoever knows this, the text says, escapes dying again. And Bhujyu falls silent. The way out of the world is narrower than a razor, and what carries you through is wind, the great breath of the cosmos. Twelve days ago, breath was the one singer the demons couldn't pierce. Here the same power, at the scale of the universe, carries a person beyond the world. It belongs to every single one of us, and to everything at once.
screen: `THE FAMILY OF KING PARIKSHIT.` · `THIRTY-TWO DAYS OF THE SUN'S CHARIOT.` · `A GAP THIN AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `WIND: EACH THING, AND ALL TOGETHER.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Notice the tiny gap at the top of each in-breath, before the out-breath begins, thinner than a fly's wing; don't hold it, just notice it each time. Then notice that the air moving through you is the same air moving through the trees outside, and the city, and the sea. Each breath yours; all breath shared.
Vayu, wind. Yajnavalkya's answer: through a gap as thin as a razor's edge, carried by vayu, each single thing and everything together.
Your line: beyond the world. Tomorrow, a practical man who wants to be shown. Until then.

howItsDone: Vayu, the wind, is honored in Hindu tradition as a deity and as the cosmic breath; in this Upanishad's debate, Yajnavalkya's answer to Bhujyu is read as praise of wind as both the individual and the whole.

original.note: Sanskrit vāyu: wind, from vā, to blow. in this answer, both each single thing (vyaṣṭi) and all together (samaṣṭi).

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle about a lost family.
what it means: the way beyond the world is razor-thin, and what carries you through is wind, the breath of everything.
what a scholar hears: 3.3.2 calls wind vyaṣṭi and samaṣṭi, the single and the whole; knowing it, one escapes punarmṛtyu, dying again.

chat.says: Where did the Parikshitas go, and how did they get there?
options: Through a gap thin as a razor's edge, Indra as a bird handed them to the wind.
They sailed across the ocean at the world's edge in the sun's own chariot.
Nobody knows; Yajnavalkya couldn't answer, so Bhujyu won that round.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya says Indra, as a bird, handed them through a razor-thin gap to the wind, which carried them to where the horse-sacrificers are.
